questions.prompt: What were they going to see tonight?
questions.passage: Except for a few downs we missed all the parade, but we would see everything tonight in the gigantic tent rising now in the park.
questions.markingGuide: Accept 'the circus' (or 'a circus show') — inferred from a 'gigantic tent... in the park', distinct from the parade already mentioned. Reject 'the parade' (that is what they already missed) or unrelated events.

questions.passage: When Scott's spade made a clanging sound he knew the stories about the buried treasure were true.
questions.markingGuide: Accept answers indicating the spade struck something metal/hard buried in the ground (e.g. 'his spade hit something metal/a box/the treasure'). Also accept a brief 'buried treasure' since it correctly identifies what was struck, even without explicitly naming the spade's contact. Reject answers unrelated to the spade hitting a buried object.

questions.passage: The roof paint was available in blue or green and Amber made her choice, knowing she wanted her house to blend in with the surrounding trees.
questions.markingGuide: Accept 'green' — trees are green, so blending in means choosing green over blue. Reject 'blue'.

questions.prompt: Why was the driver looking for a place to pull Off the road?
questions.passage: The wipers could hardly keep the windscreen clear of water. The driver looked for a place to pull off the road. The truck appeared suddenly as a massive shape swerving around the car with its horn blaring.
questions.markingGuide: Accept answers referencing heavy rain reducing visibility/making driving dangerous (e.g. 'it was raining hard and he couldn't see well'). Reject answers with no reference to rain/visibility.

questions.prompt: Why was the truck driver blaring his horn?
questions.passage: The wipers could hardly keep the windscreen clear of water. The driver looked for a place to pull off the road. The truck appeared suddenly as a massive shape swerving around the car with its horn blaring.
questions.markingGuide: Accept answers referencing warning the car of danger — the truck swerved suddenly and closely around the car in poor visibility, so the horn warned of the near-collision (e.g. 'to warn the car/because it nearly hit the car', 'because he almost crashed into them'). Reject answers that only describe road conditions (e.g. 'the road was slippery') without connecting to warning of the near-miss.

questions.passage: Sue enjoyed traveling in the car. but she could never stay still. She was constantly excited by whatever she saw, especially things frat moved. We were travelling down a quiet country road one lazy Sunday afternoon. Sue, balancing on her four short legs between the headrests of the front seat. spotted a hawk that rose up in front of the car. With a growl she lunged at it. It took several minutes for her to recover.
questions.markingGuide: Accept 'a dog' — evidenced by four legs, riding in the car, growling and lunging at the hawk. Reject other animals (e.g. 'a cat').

questions.prompt: What happened to Sue after she lunged?

questions.prompt: What was Great Auntie Mira's eyesight like?
questions.passage:
Out on the field, Great Auntie Mira screwed up her eyes and peered down the pitch as she faced Uncle Ben, the bowler. She steadied herself. The noise of the ball hitting the wooden cricket bat told her that she could now run down to the other end. The ball didn't travel far, but the young ones knew to take their time in returning it to the bowler- long enough for Mira to score a run for her team.

Another hit. Away went Great Auntie Mira. When she arrived at the other end, she was met with shouts of "Run again, Auntie! They haven't found it yet!"

She complained that she didn't see the ball coming when Uncle Jimmy's new wife Gloria had a turn, so when Uncle Jimmy bowled next, he bowled slowly.

Miraculously Uncle Jimmy's first ball hit the exact centre of Great Auntie Mira's bat. She lifted it and the ball high into the air. She started to make her way down the pitch. The nephews, nieces, aunts and uncles all suddenly stood still and watched in unbelieving silence. But it wasn't Great Auntie that they were watching.

There was a triumphant shout from behind. Mira stopped, halfway between wickets, and she too, looked back.

Uncle Jimmy's new wife had caught her out.
questions.markingGuide: Accept 'poor/bad' — evidenced by screwing up her eyes to see down the pitch, and not seeing Gloria's ball coming. Reject 'good' eyesight.
